prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets and to analyse industry dynamics, which made it possible to measure market power and welfare in real markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged. The round-1 exchange tested it and did not weaken the main points. Random-coefficients demand with endogenous prices (Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995, building on Berry's inversion) and the Ericson-Pakes dynamic-industry framework gave economists a disciplined way to recover substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data. The method produces counterfactuals, such as merger effects and the value of new products, that earlier reduced-form work could not. It is used in merger review, antitrust and regulation and has spread into trade, health, environmental and public economics. I use the chair's question on the line between a toolkit and a discovery. A contribution counts as discovery-enabling if it (a) makes a class of questions answerable that was not answerable before, (b) is validated through use and not only through theory, and (c) has spread beyond its home subfield. BLP meets all three on the evidence already cited by members. The core is about thirty years old, so maturity is not in question. The citation should stay at method level, namely demand and competition estimation in differentiated-product markets plus industry dynamics. That keeps the unit of the prize clear and puts the BLP authors, the identifiable originators of the estimator, in the three slots. I also tested the case against my own standard. The attribution is easier to defend than for B013, B050 or B049, and I do not rely on support counts as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still toolkit versus discovery. A Committee that wants a substantive finding about the economy could reasonably prefer another entry. A second reservation is that BLP-type applied results are sensitive to numerical implementation, instrument choice and functional form. Supporters say these problems are documented and largely addressed, but that rests on our background knowledge. If merger-simulation predictions had been shown to fail systematically in retrospective evaluations, or if conclusions on welfare and market power flipped under reasonable alternative specifications, I would weaken my support. The third reservation is attribution. Any three-name cut leaves out Bresnahan, whose claim on the empirical-IO agenda is serious, and leaves out Reiss, Benkard and Levin. A method-level citation also leaves much of Pakes's production-function and dynamic-games work as context and not as the stated basis of the award. Finally, I am the chair and an explicit B001 supporter, so the Committee should discount my summary of the other positions to that extent.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Pakes and Berry but names Bresnahan as the third laureate, on the grounds that the achievement is wider than the BLP paper: market-power estimation, production-function methods and dynamic models. He sees Bresnahan's early differentiated-product demand work as the foundation of the programme and says Levinsohn's role is largely captured in a single paper. He accepts that a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan argument seriously, and your concession that the Levinsohn version is not an error narrows our disagreement. I still prefer Levinsohn, for two reasons. First, the precise and testable claim to credit is the estimator, and the estimator has three named originators. If Levinsohn is left out and Berry stays in, the single jointly authored result is split. Second, the wider lineage you describe, which includes Olley-Pakes, Ericson-Pakes and the new empirical IO, cannot be credited with three names without producing exclusions larger than Levinsohn's. A programme-level citation would therefore need either more people than the cap allows or a different cut. If the Committee chose that framing I would not obstruct it, but I would then ask for the citation to be reworded around the agenda and not around BLP. Under a method-level citation I would stay with Levinsohn.

responses.point: Stromberg asks whether a single-achievement configuration is best or whether a second achievement could be added within the three-person limit without weakening the citation. He also notes that Naming Levinsohn rather than Bresnahan could be read as favouring one paper over the broader agenda.
responses.response: I would keep a single achievement. A second achievement would have to take one of the three slots, and the only natural donor is the BLP trio itself. That would split a compact credit unit to make room for a part with its own attribution problems. The cap also means a two-part prize would give each part one or two names, which is a weaker citation for both. On your reading about Levinsohn and Bresnahan, I accept that it is a fair way to describe the choice. I think it is the right choice for a method-level citation, because the prize names the people who produced the specific method, and the agenda that made it possible is credited in the narrative around the prize and not through the laureate list.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. She rejects my round-1 two-name Autor-Hanson version because dropping Katz removes the part of the programme with the longest confirmation. She also treats B001 as the strongest alternative and values B013 for its link between framework and credible identification.
responses.response: Your objection to the two-name version is fair. Autor-Hanson was a way of resting the award on the trade-shock evidence, and it does leave out the wage-structure work with the longest record. It was an alternative, not my preferred configuration, and I do not defend it as the better B013 design. The central difficulty remains the one you name yourself. The Committee would have to decide whether the achievement is one strand or two, and then choose between Katz and Dorn. I also remain cautious about maturity, since the persistence of the China-shock effects and the AI-era relevance are still developing. I would support B013 as an alternative if B001 fails, but I would want it settled first which strand the citation rests on.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B050 first with Melitz and Helpman. He treats Melitz (2003) as the origin and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple as a constitutive extension. He accepts that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Redding are an attribution cost and treats B001 as a close alternative.
responses.response: I weigh your view with care because we are co-authors and IIES colleagues, and I do not defer to it. On substance, you answer the 2008 overlap well. Selection and reallocation across firms is a different discovery from increasing returns and location. That is why I now list B050 as one of my alternatives in place of B049. My remaining hesitation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the entry, and a two-name award would credit Melitz and Helpman for an idea that other authors developed in parallel. A Melitz-only version would be cleaner on origin but would leave out Helpman's FDI-versus-exporting work, which you correctly call constitutive. Neither version is free of cost. For me B050 is a serious second-tier option and does not overtake B001 on attribution.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B002 to B001 after reading the openings. He says he is now less confident in his own three-name B002 trio and treats B002 and B013 as strong alternatives that B001's lead should not be read as a verdict on.
responses.response: I agree that B001's position is not a scientific verdict on B002 or B013, and that is the standard I have tried to apply. On B002 I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clean pair. I would answer the chair's question by saying that the distinct ground relative to the 2022 prize is the general-equilibrium collateral-constraint mechanism and its amplification of shocks, and not bank runs or the financial accelerator. It is still a harder claim to defend than B001, because the 2022 recognition is close in subject and the empirical identification of the collateral channel is model-dependent. I keep B002 as my first alternative with two names, and I would not add Gertler just to reach three.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation (BLP trio) or a programme-level citation (new empirical IO), which would change the third name and the wording.
Whether the Committee treats a measurement and estimation toolkit as a sufficient discovery. I have stated my criterion, but others may weigh it differently.

How far applied BLP-type results are robust to numerical implementation, instruments and functional form. This rests on background knowledge, and evidence of systematic retrospective failure of merger-simulation predictions would reduce my confidence.
Whether the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version of B002 leaves enough distinct ground relative to the 2022 prize.
I have not independently verified citation, adoption or regulatory-use claims, and I rely on the round-1 files and my own background knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosed from my profile, not adjudicated. I have co-authored with Per Krusell (secretary), Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. The 2018 Scientific Background cites my own climate work with Golosov, Krusell and Tsyvinski. None of these ties involves a credited name on B001, B002 or B050, and no connection to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Bresnahan, Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman is apparent from the supplied profile. As chair I also wrote the round-1 summary and am an explicit B001 supporter, so members should read it with that in mind. Krusell and Friberg prefer B001, and Boppart prefers B050, so these ties do not point in a single direction.
